\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q13, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=13, type=multi, subtopic={Force on wires}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: net force and torque on a square coil in a given nonuniform field | steps: force on each side F = I L x B; sum of four; torque about centre; check options}]
Figure shows a square current carrying coil of edge length $L$. The magnetic field on the coil is given by $\vec B=\dfrac{B_0y}{L}\hat i+\dfrac{B_0x}{L}\hat j$ where $B_0$ is a positive constant. ($A$ is area of coil)
\bfig{71.1}{SI01_p1_phy_s2_q13_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If coil is free to rotate about $x$ axis torque on the coil is given by $\dfrac12iAB_0\hat i$.}
\opt{B}{If coil is free to rotate about $y$ - axis torque on coil is given by $-\dfrac12iAB_0\hat j$.}
\opt{C}{Resultant force on coil is zero.}
\opt{D}{Equation for the torque $\vec\mu\times\vec B$ where $\mu$ is magnetic moment of coil is not valid on the coil if any of the side is fixed as axis.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI04-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 04 (14 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Biot-Savart}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: field, flux for a spiral loop of N turns | steps: turns distributed over radii a to b; field at centre by integration over rings; mutual inductance or flux; check | I: integrate ring contributions with uniform turn density}]
Consider a spiral loop of inner radius a \& outer radius b, made up of N turns of fine close wires with current I. O is center of spiral. P is a point on axis of spiral such that outer \& inner radius makes angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ \& $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ on that point.
\bfig{134.5}{SI04_p1_phy_s1_q02_A.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$B_P=\dfrac{\mu_0 iN}{(b-a)}\left[\ell n\left(\dfrac{\left(2-\sqrt3\right)}{\sqrt3}\right)-\dfrac12\left(\sqrt3-1\right)\right]$}
\opt{B}{$B_P=\dfrac{\mu_0 iN}{2(b-a)}\left[\ell n\left(\dfrac{\left(2+\sqrt3\right)}{\sqrt3}\right)-\dfrac12\left(\sqrt3-1\right)\right]$}
\opt{C}{$B_O=\dfrac{\mu_0 iN}{(b-a)}\ell n\left(\sqrt{\dfrac ba}\right)$}
\opt{D}{$B_O=\dfrac{\mu_0 iN}{(b-a)}\ell n\left(\dfrac ba\right)$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI04-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 04 (14 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Force on wires}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: force or field from two fixed parallel long wires on a moving wire | steps: fields of two wires superpose; position dependence; force on the loop AB; check statements | I: superpose fields of two parallel wires}]
PP$'$ and QQ$'$ are two fixed infinite long straight wire both parallel to $z$ axis, with current I in each wire, ABCD is a square loop of side $2\ell$. Sides AD and BC are parallel to $z$ axis \& AB is in $xy$ plane and, CD is in plane parallel to $x$-$y$ plane.
\bfig{84.0}{SI04_p1_phy_s1_q03_1.png}
PP$'$ and QQ$'$ are cutting $x$-axis at $(-a,0,0)$ and $(a,0,0)$ and $2\ell<2a$. ABCD loop is free to rotate about $z$-axis only which is passing in it's plane from center of ABCD loop. Side AB of loop is making angle $\phi$ with $x$-axis. Choose correct statements.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Torque on ABCD loop along $z$ axis in situation when $\phi=0$ is zero.}
\opt{B}{Torque on ABCD loop along $z$ axis in situation when $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is zero.}
\opt{C}{Torque on ABCD loop along $z$ axis in situation when $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is $\dfrac{4\mu_0 I^2\ell^2 a}{\pi\left(a^2+\ell^2\right)}$.}
\opt{D}{Torque on ABCD loop along $z$ axis in situation when $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is maximum.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI04-P1-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={Score-I - Test 04 (14 Jan 2022)}, questions={9-10}]
Arrangement shown below has an electron source producing electrons of various speed emitted along line of $x$-axis. Region-I is sufficiently large in dimensions to work as velocity selector. It contain uniform \& constant with time, magnetic field of strength B and electric field of strength E, which are along $-\hat k$ and $-\hat j$ direction as shown.

Region-II contain uniform magnetic field of same direction \& strength $-B\hat k$ as in region-I but it can be switched on \& off, after electrons have entered by some distance in region-II. [Charge of e$^-$ is $e$ (magnitude) \& mass $=m$]
\bfig{208.0}{SI04_p1_phy_s2_para9_10_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA13-P2-PHY-S4-G3-4, source={Score Advanced - Test 13 (13 May 2023)}, questions={3-4}]
A railgun is an electrically powered electromagnetic projectile launcher based on similar principles to the homopolar motor. It comprises a pair of parallel conducting rails, along which a sliding armature is accelerated by the electromagnetic effects of a current that flows down one rail, into the armature and then back along the other rail.\par
Now two parallel metal rails are connected to an electrical power supply. When a conductive projectile is inserted between the rails (at the end connected to the power supply), it completes the circuit. Electrons flow from the negative terminal of the power supply up the negative rail, across the projectile, and down the positive rail, back to the power supply.\par
This current makes the railgun behave as an electromagnet, creating a magnetic field inside the loop formed by the length of the rails up to the position of the armature. In accordance with the right-hand rule, the magnetic field circulates around each conductor. Since the current is in the opposite direction along each rail, the net magnetic field between the rails (B) is directed at right angles to the plane formed by the central axes of the rails and the armature. In combination with the current (I) in the armature, this produces a Lorentz force which accelerates the projectile along the rails, away from the power supply.\par
If radius of the rails is 1 mm (which are assumed to be circular in cross section) , the distance between the centre points of the rails is 1 m and the constant current through the system is 10A. ($\ell$n 10 = $\dfrac{7}{3}$)\par
\bfig{118.8}{SA13_p2_phy_s4_para3_4_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}

In order to further increase the energy of the cyclotron, scientists built a ``sector- shaped focusing cyclotron''. During the sector-shaped focusing process, ions can rotate periodically in a closed equilibrium orbit at a constant speed.\par
A simplified diagram of the fan-shaped focusing magnetic field distribution is shown in the figure. The circular area with the mouth at the center is equally divided into six fan- shaped areas, three of which are peak areas and three are valley areas. The peak areas and valley areas are alternately distributed. In the peak area, there is a uniform magnetic field with a direction perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The magnetic induction intensity is B. There is no magnetic field in the valley area. Positive ions with mass m and charge q rotate at a constant speed v. Their closed equilibrium orbit is shown by the dotted line in the figure.\par
\bfig{116.5}{SA23_p1_phy_s2_q10_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The radius of orbit in closed equilibrium orbit in peak area is $\dfrac{mv}{qB}$.}
\opt{B}{The time period of ions rotating around the closed equilibrium orbit is $\dfrac{(2\pi+3\sqrt3)m}{qB}$.}
\opt{C}{The centre angle of the arc ($\theta$) of the orbit in peak area is $\dfrac\pi3$.}
\opt{D}{Now a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the paper plane is also applied in the valley area. The magnetic induction intensity is B$'$. The central angle of the new closed equilibrium orbit (as found in option (C)) in a peak area is now 90$^\circ$. The ratio $\dfrac{B'}{B}$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
